summary:
Turn real-world observations into testable worlds.

Every satellite sees a different version of the same Earth. NASA has tracked wildfires for over 25 years, but its instruments detect fires differently. When a newer satellite sees four times as many hotspots, does that mean four times as many fires, or a sharper view?

Isogon models the fire activity behind those measurements. Drawing on 548 million NASA detections, our scientific world model estimates how activity changes across space and time and predicts what MODIS and VIIRS would observe. Explore the results on a 3D Earth and compare decades of activity through one harmonized fire calendar.

A reconstruction only matters if it can be tested. In Isogon's experimental environment, we hide VIIRS observations, predict what it would detect, then reveal the actual measurements. Across 57 held-out fires, our model reduced prediction error by 40% against a MODIS-only baseline; cross-sensor disagreement fell from 78% to 14%.

This helps scientists compare fire seasons without mistaking improved detection for increased burning. Next, we're exploring learned agents that choose which measurements would most reduce uncertainty.

Wildfire is the first application. Isogon's larger goal is to build scientific world models that reconstruct physical systems, test their predictions, and guide the next observation.
details:
What it does

Isogon turns real-world observations into testable worlds.

NASA has tracked wildfires for over 25 years, but its satellites do not see fire the same way. VIIRS detects small fires that MODIS misses and reports about four times as many detections over the same years, so trends across the two are hard to compare. Isogon estimates the fire activity behind those measurements and models how each instrument would observe it, creating one consistent record across decades.

How it works

Isogon has three parts.

A scientific world model works at two scales. Globally, it puts 548 million NASA FIRMS detections from 238 countries and territories on one scale, month by month since 2000. Fire by fire, it estimates where fire was on the ground and predicts what MODIS and VIIRS would each report, given each sensor’s pixel size, pass times and sensitivity. Every estimate carries an uncertainty range that we test: on years that did not set it, the 80% range held 79% of the time.

An experimental environment makes the model testable. It withholds one satellite, predicts what it should detect, then reveals the real measurements and scores the difference.

A learning agent is our experimental research component. It chooses which observations would most improve the model, and visitors can play the same round against it.

All of it lives in an interactive 3D Earth. Watch 25 years of fire on one scale, draw a box anywhere to read its harmonized fire calendar, or fly into a real fire over real terrain and see the estimate through each satellite’s eyes.

Results

Harmonization: with each year hidden in turn across 5,227 regions, Isogon’s estimate from MODIS misses VIIRS’s real monthly count by 14%. Uncorrected, the miss is 78%. A single conversion ratio per region, the usual approach, leaves 18%.

Prediction: the fire-level model was fitted on one set of fires and tested on others kept apart. On 57 unseen fires across six continents, chosen by a rule fixed before any result was seen and scored once, it matched VIIRS 40% better than MODIS alone.

Live: 35 predictions have been sealed before the satellite pass, each with a SHA-256 fingerprint and time in our seal log, and each is scored when NASA’s data arrives.

Benefits and Impact:

Isogon helps scientists, land managers and researchers compare decades of wildfire activity without confusing better satellite detection with increased burning. Its harmonized calendar makes it possible to examine seasonal patterns, identify unusual years, and investigate how much of an apparent trend comes from the instruments rather than the Earth.

Wildfire is the first application of a broader scientific approach: reconstruct physical systems from imperfect measurements, test predictions against unseen observations, and learn which experiments provide the most useful evidence.

What makes it creative

Most harmonization ends in a corrected table. Isogon ends in a world you can question. Hiding a satellite and revealing the truth turns validation into something anyone can watch.

What we considered

Honesty came first. Test fires were fixed before we looked, each test was run once, and results that went against us stay on the page: our first model lost on exact overlap, and today’s agent is not yet better than a simple rule. We used only open data, and we made the public site run with no server and no paid service, so anyone can open it and check our work.

Tools

NASA FIRMS active fire data (MODIS and VIIRS), NASA CMR for satellite pass times, NASA Blue Marble, and open terrain imagery from USGS, USDA and Sentinel-2. The model is written from scratch in Python with numpy and Pillow, with no machine learning framework. The interface is TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js. Pyodide runs the same Python model inside the visitor’s browser. Hosted on GitHub Pages, built on one laptop.

Wildfire is Isogon’s first application. We’re developing a broader approach to scientific world modeling: reconstruct physical systems from measurements, test predictions against unseen observations, and learn which experiments provide the most useful evidence.
